Lessons.Title: Solutions to Inequalities in One Variable
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: find and interpret the entire solution set of a one-variable inequality using reasoning, a related equation, substitution and a correctly marked number line. Independent Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L19, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/19/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). The source includes reasoning about an orchard trip and optional technology work; do not reduce the range of values to a single answer.

Original adaptation of an orchard choice: Orchard A costs $9 per student and requires three paid adult chaperones; Orchard B costs $10 per student and only one paid chaperone. For s≥0 integer students, totals A=9(s+3), B=10(s+1). A is cheaper when 9s+27<10s+10, hence s>17. Exactly s=17 gives equal costs, and with fewer than 17 students B is cheaper.

A separate inequality 7(3−x)>14 holds when dividing positive 7 to obtain 3−x>2, hence x<1. The related equation has boundary x=1; this point is not included because the sign is strict. On a number line draw an open circle at 1 and a ray leftward. At x=0 the original yields 21>14; at x=1, 14>14 is false.

Student task: derive both inequality ranges, show at least three substitution trials around each boundary, draw two labeled number lines, interpret integer restrictions for students and critique whether equality should be allowed. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): variable and inequality model, correct open/closed boundary, positive/negative and integer tests, contextual explanation and critique.

KeyConcepts.Title: Solution set
KeyConcepts.Definition: An inequality usually has a range of solutions, not just one number.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Specify endpoints and open versus closed boundaries.

KeyConcepts.Title: Related equation boundary
KeyConcepts.Definition: The corresponding equality locates the candidate transition point.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Test points on both sides to find the direction.

KeyConcepts.Title: Integer context
KeyConcepts.Definition: Counts of students are whole and nonnegative.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Intersect the real interval with the permissible domain.

WorkedExamples.Title: Solve and graph a strict inequality
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve 7(3−x)>14.
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: Open circle at 1 and shade left.
WorkedExamples.Check: At x=1 original equality 14>14 is false.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare two orchard offers
WorkedExamples.Question: When is 9(s+3)<10(s+1)?
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A cheaper for 18 or more students; equal at 17.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish test values
WorkedExamples.Question: Is x=−2,1,3 a solution of 7(3−x)>14?
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: All results match solution range x<1.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Only x=−2 among listed values is a solution.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Failing to reverse inequality when multiplying by −1
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The order relation reverses for negative scaling.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Including a strict boundary in the solution set
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use an open point and check the boundary.

SummaryPoints: One-variable inequalities usually define intervals or rays.
The related equation identifies the boundary, but test values determine the correct side.
Orchard A is cheaper for at least 18 students; at 17 the prices match.
Graphs, model reasoning and interpretation require teacher review.
